recent_posts.title: Start a tech blog and get paid $20
recent_posts.summary: An open call encouraging developers to start their own tech blogs, with a financial incentive ($20 for the first post, another $20 for three more within six months). The offer requires publishing on an open-source platform (not Medium), with recommendations like write.as, Jekyll, or Hugo with GitHub Pages. A curated list of blogs started through this initiative is included, along with a Free Writers Club mailing list for ongoing support.

recent_posts.title: Drew DeVault's Japanese Learning Resources
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault shares a self-directed Japanese language learning guide covering kanji, vocabulary, grammar, reading, writing, listening, speaking, and conversation skills. Key advice includes avoiding romaji, using Anki for spaced-repetition memorization, following Tae Kim's grammar guide, and studying kanji in RTK order before switching to vocabulary-focused study around 300-400 kanji. Pre-built Anki decks for JLPT levels and common vocabulary are provided, along with custom deck generators. The guide emphasizes identifying personal goals and treating each language skill as a discrete area requiring individual attention.

recent_posts.title: tar: a slop-free alternative to rsync
recent_posts.summary: A short practical guide showing how to use tar piped over SSH as a simpler alternative to rsync for transferring files between hosts. Covers the key tar flags (-c, -x, -z, -C, -f), explains path handling logic, and shows how to add a progress display using pv. Also mentions a small wrapper tool called xtar that simplifies the workflow.

recent_posts.title: A eulogy for Vim
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault reflects on his deep personal relationship with Vim and mourns its direction after Bram Moolenaar's death, particularly the adoption of LLMs and AI-generated code in both Vim and NeoVim development. He criticizes generative AI broadly for its environmental, social, and political harms. In response, he has forked Vim as 'Vim Classic', based on Vim 8.2.0148 (just before Vim9 Script), backporting security patches and bug fixes while keeping the codebase AI-free. He invites contributors to help maintain it.

recent_posts.title: The cults of TDD and GenAI
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault draws a parallel between the cult of TDD and the current enthusiasm for AI coding agents. He argues that TDD, while useful in parts, creates a false sense of productivity through dopamine-driven metrics like coverage percentages and green test suites, without guaranteeing that software actually meets real requirements. He then extends this critique to AI coding agents, suggesting they offer a similar psychological rush — letting mediocre programmers feel like 10x engineers — while producing architecturally unsound code. The post closes with a broader critique of AI's environmental and societal costs, arguing that the emotional appeal of feeling 'great' at programming blinds people to these externalities.

recent_posts.title: Redesigning my microkernel from the ground up
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault shares the redesign of his microkernel project, now called Hermes, built in the Hare programming language. After his previous microkernel Helios stalled due to design flaws, he spent two years researching OS design, writing a Unix clone (Bunnix), and rethinking core architecture. Hermes introduces symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) with a simple per-CPU work-stealing scheduler under 200 lines of code, a redesigned syscall and IPC ABI, reference counting instead of seL4-style capability derivation graphs for resource management, and a port of the upstream Hare standard library for userspace. The kernel has been tested on roughly ten real hardware devices and a downloadable ISO is available for testing.

recent_posts.title: FUTO misrepresents donations as grants and platforms fascist figures
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault investigates FUTO, an organization claiming to fund open source software. He finds that their 'grant program' is misleading: rather than formal grants, FUTO made small, quiet donations (e.g., $1,000 to musl libc via GitHub Sponsors) and then displayed the logos of well-known projects like ffmpeg, VLC, NeoVim, and Wireshark on their homepage without authorization, implying endorsements that were never given. Multiple maintainers confirmed they had no knowledge of any grant. Beyond the deceptive branding, DeVault criticizes FUTO for platforming Curtis Yarvin, a self-proclaimed fascist, through interviews and a staged debate with Louis Rossmann. He argues FUTO uses open-washing tactics and fascist-adjacent associations to legitimize itself, and calls on affected projects to demand removal of their logos. An update notes FUTO revised their website to clarify donations vs. grants but declined to address the Yarvin platforming issue.

recent_posts.title: Cloudflare sponsors open source projects led by figures accused of fascism
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault criticizes Cloudflare's decision to sponsor two open source projects — Ladybird browser and Omarchy (a pre-configured Arch Linux distribution) — arguing that both are led by individuals he identifies as fascists. He points to tweets and blog posts from Ladybird's Andreas Kling and Omarchy's David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) as evidence of far-right views, including endorsements of white replacement theory, tributes to Charlie Kirk, and alignment with Elon Musk's politics. DeVault questions why Cloudflare is directing hundreds of thousands of dollars to these projects rather than the underlying projects they build upon.

recent_posts.title: What a secure JavaScript ecosystem could look like and why it probably won't happen
recent_posts.summary: In the wake of a major npm supply-chain attack, the JavaScript ecosystem has an opportunity to fundamentally reform its dependency management practices. The author outlines what a better future could look like: a real standard library to eliminate micro-dependencies, Linux-distro-style package curation with maintainers and trust relationships, universal package signatures, reproducible builds, and corporate investment in sustainable open source security. However, the author is deeply pessimistic, predicting the community will respond with only symbolic gestures like mandatory 2FA and token donations, repeating the same cycle that has played out for decades without meaningful change.

recent_posts.title: Embedding Wren in Hare
recent_posts.summary: Drew DeVault introduces hare-wren, a library that embeds the Wren scripting language into Hare programs. The post covers the motivation for choosing Wren over Lua, demonstrates basic usage including calling Hare from Wren and vice versa via foreign methods, and describes an optional wren::api submodule providing an async runtime, a modest standard library (file I/O, process args/env), and a module loader. A command-line tool hwren is also included, though without REPL support.
